title: Lessons From Our Exes: 5 Red Flags We Ignored
summary: Cherie and Jean share five lessons from their own past relationships, each paired with a business lesson: don't put people on a pedestal (the halo effect), mind the age gap (life stage and power imbalance), date for track record not money (financial resilience), don't date coworkers or work with best friends without preparing for the fallout, and beware love bombing by setting calibrated boundaries. The through-line is that every relationship is a set of data points, and that charisma is not credibility in love or business.

ideas.idea: Do not put anyone on a pedestal: once you decide someone is extraordinary, you edit out every reason they are not.
ideas.detail: Jean dated a cancer survivor whose story made her assume maturity and morality; she ignored him telling her she'd be 'perfect at 112 lbs', pressuring her to quit her job, and cheating with an ex-girlfriend Jean had even lent a designer dress to. Friends said she was 'so out of his league', which people only say when they mean it.

ideas.idea: The pedestal in business is the halo effect: one impressive trait, like charisma or a Stanford-dropout pedigree, outshines all the red flags and people stop doing diligence.
ideas.detail: Elizabeth Holmes was pattern-matched to Zuckerberg and Jobs as a dropout (the show about her is literally called The Dropout) and Adam Neumann was treated as god-like, while everyone ignored how they behaved inside their companies. When the story gets too good, people stop doing emotional or investor diligence.

ideas.idea: Mentors and managers are just people with faults; putting them on a pedestal early in your career sets you up for guaranteed disappointment.
ideas.detail: Cherie notes that even someone great on stage with strong presence will disappoint if you expect them to live out a grand vision you built for them.

ideas.idea: Pedestal check exercise: ask whether you like the person or the idea of them, name the prevailing reason for the pedestal, then tally their actions for and against that attribute.
ideas.detail: Ask what you like beyond resume values like job, school or accolades, and whether they've exhibited traits that make you independently respect them. Jean says she wishes she had done this tally.

ideas.idea: Mind the age gap: what matters is not the number of years but the life stage, and when you are the younger woman a power imbalance is baked in whether or not the other person exerts it.
ideas.detail: Cherie at 19-20 dated a Harvard grad 4 years older working at McKinsey who became half boyfriend, half mentor; she second- and triple-guessed everything she said and it failed because she was so in her head, even though he was kind. The older person inherently has more financial power, life experience and emotional leverage.

ideas.idea: Listen to your gut when something feels off in a power-imbalanced situation, even if you can't name it yet.
ideas.detail: At 20, Jean went on a ski date with a 33-year-old ex-Goldman hedge fund founder she met at a Tuck private equity conference at Dartmouth; at his house (with taxidermy) she felt 'I'm not in control' and left. At 37 she says dating a 13-year gap would be fine because both are formed adults.

ideas.idea: Age gap relationships work best when both people are fully formed adults with financial independence and strong boundaries; timing matters more than the number.
ideas.detail: Financial independence matters so you never feel you owe the other person for what they provide, especially when you are in a vulnerable state.

ideas.idea: Reverse ageism at work: don't grant credibility to the older engineer or MD just because they are older; build your own confidence so you can be peers.
ideas.detail: Deference should be earned by someone proving they are legit, not by seniority in years; this varies by industry.

ideas.idea: Don't date for money, date for track record: ask whether you'd still date them if they lost it all, because resilience and ambition let them rebuild.
ideas.detail: Look for trajectory, not current status; you want someone who can build wealth with you, not just someone who has it. A June 2025 National Library of Medicine study of 3,700 households found financial resilience buffers the negative effects of economic setbacks on happiness and mental health, and 'every 10 years something happens that has never happened before.'
names_or_cases: National Library of Medicine study (June 2025, 3,700 households)

ideas.idea: No money is ever free: inherited or family wealth always comes with conditions that invisibly shape a person's life decisions, so dig into it if you date someone expecting an inheritance.
ideas.detail: Cherie has seen multimillionaire heirs build their lives around money they know is coming, and only in the relationship does it become clear that decisions are driven by the money's stipulations. Wealth not earned through hardship may not have shaped character.

ideas.idea: Partner attributes to look for over time: resilience, discipline and work ethic, long-term thinking, ability to rebuild after setbacks, plus loyalty, integrity and character.
ideas.detail: These can only be observed after being with someone through uncomfortable or challenging situations. Loyalty applies if you yourself are a loyal person.

ideas.idea: Treat dating like a scientist collecting data points: zoom out of your own head and observe why the person acts as they do and how you react, because decisions should be about what makes you happy.
ideas.detail: Character reveals itself when you bring something up or ask follow-up questions in a challenging situation. Every relationship is data on where your boundaries are and when you speak up.

ideas.idea: Don't shit where you eat: workplace relationships bring power imbalance, reputation consequences and emotional fallout, and breakups don't stay inside the bubble.
ideas.detail: One third of US workers have dated a coworker (SHRM); a 2024 SHRM survey found 68% of HR professionals cite favoritism perceptions and 61% cite conflicts of interest as top concerns. Cherie dated someone at her first job on a different team and was distracted worrying about running into him in the cafe when she wanted to focus on her career.

ideas.idea: If you do date a coworker later in your career, discuss what happens if you break up up front, like a prenup for the workplace relationship.
ideas.detail: Timing matters: more mature people at the same company can make it work, but young people have no space for the mess and drama at work.

ideas.idea: Don't cofound or hire your best friend unless you're prepared for the consequences: the shorthand and inherent trust that make the friendship strong lead to looser contracts and undefined expectations.
ideas.detail: Friends assume they're on the same page and skip defining things they'd define with a stranger. 'It's not personal, it's business' can never be true with a friend. One of Cherie's best friends refuses to hire friends because she values the friendship too much.

ideas.idea: Beware the love bomber: an 8-hour first date followed by a drop-in visit days later is a red flag, even when it's the person's natural salesperson personality rather than deliberate manipulation.
ideas.detail: Jean, fresh out of an 8-year engagement, didn't clock the intensity because she was used to daily contact with a live-in fiance. Only when she saw the guy charm her friends did she realize being loved by everyone was his default mode, and that he was a self-described people pleaser.

ideas.idea: Moments of apartness early in dating are when you can actually evaluate how you feel; love bombing removes them and feels amazing, which is exactly why you need a pause.
ideas.detail: Being love bombed makes you feel like the best person in the world and critical thinking and the prefrontal cortex go out the window.

ideas.idea: Know your own boundaries (physical, time, emotional) before entering a relationship, especially if you know you seek external validation, or the other person will lead you wherever they want.
ideas.detail: Cherie admits she is susceptible to 'you're obsessed with me, I love this' due to growing up with immigrant parents, so she needs to know herself and her boundaries first.

ideas.idea: Don't carry boundaries calibrated for a long-term relationship into a new one; new people must unlock levels of access by earning trust over time.
ideas.detail: Jean gave a brand-new partner the lax boundaries that took 8 years of trust to build with her ex. Exercise: pre-define what behavior is acceptable at a first date, seven dates, six months, and so on.

ideas.idea: In business and love, charisma is not credibility: apply the same skepticism to an overselling suitor that you'd apply to an overhyped product ('prove it, where's the free trial').
ideas.detail: Trust the people who build slowly and consistently over time; be as discerning with your time, emotions and body as you are with your money.
